title: Westlaw and Lexis cost per search: how out-of-plan charges add up on a Mac in 2026
metaTitle: Westlaw and Lexis cost per search: out-of-plan charges
description: Westlaw's help page lists no dollar amount for out-of-plan charges. Learn how these charges work, what they cost firms, and free fixes for Mac lawyers.
targetKeyword: westlaw and lexis cost per search
intro: The Westlaw help page lists no dollar amount for out-of-plan charges, so you cannot read a per-search price off it. Your real cost depends on your plan, the documents you open, and the rates in your subscriber pricing guide. Below you will find how these charges work, what they cost firms, and fixes you can start on your Mac today.
tldr: Out-of-plan charges bill documents that fall outside your subscription plan. The Westlaw help page gives no dollar amounts. Your rate comes from your subscriber pricing guide.
Clicking into a document can trigger a charge. A library guide says browsing the table of contents avoids the per-search charge.
Citator reports can carry charges when you click documents from them. Some Westlaw plans charge extra for KeyCite.
Firms bill computerized research at cost less often than they used to. Track each session with a Client ID and a short research log.

blocks.text: Why Westlaw and Lexis cost per search is hard to pin down

Westlaw's help page defines out-of-plan charges as document charges outside your subscription plan. They apply when you retrieve or deliver documents your plan does not include. The page says the rates follow the subscriber pricing guide. It lists no dollar amounts, so public pages will not give you a number to budget from.

A law library guide from Florida Coastal describes a per-search charge that you can avoid by browsing the table of contents. That tells you the risk sits in the documents you open. Your cost is the count of out-of-plan documents, times the rate in your guide, plus any citator line on your plan.
A worked example for your own matter

Suppose you run a session with several searches, open a few documents, and run one KeyCite check. Assume your plan covers the searches but not every document. Count the documents that fall outside your plan. Multiply that count by the rate in your pricing guide. Add the KeyCite line if your plan charges extra for it. That total is the session cost.
Write the rate once in your research log. Then you never have to redo the math from scratch, and billing can check your figure against the statement in a minute.

blocks.title: Clicks are the meter
blocks.text: Every document click is a possible out-of-plan charge. Results lists invite you to open everything in new tabs. Before you click, decide whether you need the full text now or can read it later.
Why many firms no longer bill research at cost

A State Bar of Wisconsin article from October 2014 says many firms now see computerized legal research as a cost of doing business. It cites an ABA Legal Technology Survey trend. Firms billing clients at cost for computerized research is decreasing, the article says. It also cites American Lawyer Media's Law Librarian Survey, which reports AmLaw 200 firms recovering less each year since 2005.

The cost-recovery rule is older than that trend. The article describes ABA Formal Opinion 93-379, issued in 1993, as allowing recovery of reasonably incurred expenses, including computer research. It also says firms on fixed-fee contracts must pass savings to clients. Your state rules, your engagement letter, and firm policy still decide what you can bill.
Questions to ask billing this week

items: Which subscriber pricing guide applies to our research plan?
What does one out-of-plan document cost under that guide?
Does printing from the browser change the charge on our plan?
Do we bill out-of-plan research to clients, and where is that written?
Who checks Client IDs before a research bill closes?
Can we get a monthly report of research charges by Client ID?

blocks.text: Mistakes that make research charges worse

items: Opening every result in a new tab before you read the list.
Leaving the Client ID blank, or using one ID for every matter.
Running the same search each week instead of setting an alert.
Clicking through a citator report without checking your plan line.
Using a per-search figure from a blog as your firm's rate.

blocks.text: The first two mistakes are hard to spot later. A statement shows the charge, but not which click caused it. Fix them before the session starts, not after the bill arrives.
Edge cases: fixed fees, pro bono, and older Lexis terms

On a fixed-fee matter, research spend comes out of your margin. The Wisconsin article says firms on fixed-fee contracts must pass savings to clients. That makes a clean research record useful. You can show where the time and charges went when a client asks.

Unbilled matters still cost the firm money. Use the matter code your firm assigns, even when no client pays for the work. That keeps the charge on the right matter in your records. Ask your billing lead which code applies.

The Florida Coastal guide says Lexis Advance had no document delivery fee. Lexis products have changed since then, and a library guide is not a price list. Ask for current terms in writing before you plan around them.
Set up a research log in Word on Mac

Open Word and choose Insert > Table to build a table. Give it columns for date, Client ID, database, documents opened, and reason. Save one file per month in the folder your firm approves. Keep client names out of the file unless your firm's data rules allow them.

Dictate each row with Hold fn, then read it before you save. Dictation works at the cursor in Word and most other apps. If you draft the cover email in Outlook, see [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook). For review settings, [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word) covers Track Changes and clause review.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a field is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do a task, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

It does not click for you. It does not log in to Westlaw or Lexis, and it cannot read your plan terms or price a session. Its research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, separate from your firm's accounts. Treat it as a second pair of eyes on the screen, not as a billing system.

blocks.title: Client data comes first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on client and patient data. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Ask your firm before you share matter details with any AI tool.
The Pro and Power plans, and a free Pro trial with no credit card, are on the [pricing page](/pricing). Dictation is unlimited on both plans. Check the page for current terms before you decide.

faq.question: What does a Westlaw or Lexis search cost per search?
faq.answer: The Westlaw help page gives no dollar amount. Rates follow the subscriber pricing guide for your plan, so that guide is the source to use. Ask your firm's research or billing lead for it. Do not budget from blog figures, because they are not sourced.

faq.question: Does a search itself trigger an out-of-plan charge?
faq.answer: Out-of-plan charges apply when you retrieve or deliver documents outside your plan. A library guide describes a per-search charge that browsing the table of contents avoids. Treat opening documents as the main risk, then check your plan terms to confirm what your firm pays.

faq.question: Does printing avoid the charge?
faq.answer: The Florida Coastal library guide says printing from the browser avoids document delivery fees. It does not say printing avoids every out-of-plan charge. Confirm with your plan before you assume printing is free.

faq.question: Can our firm bill out-of-plan research to a client?
faq.answer: ABA Formal Opinion 93-379 allows recovery of reasonably incurred expenses, including computer research, according to a 2014 State Bar of Wisconsin article. Your state rules, your engagement letter, and firm policy decide the rest. Ask your ethics counsel if you are unsure.

faq.question: What is a Client ID for in Westlaw and Lexis?
faq.answer: Tulane Law Library's FAQ says the Client ID tracks which client to bill for a research session. Enter it before each session, and use one ID per matter. A wrong ID bills the wrong client.

faq.question: Can Lazur run Westlaw or Lexis for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can answer questions about what is on screen, point at a field, and dictate notes. Its research jobs run in its own Chrome tabs, not in your firm's accounts.

faq.question: Is it safe to use AI tools with research on client matters?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Still follow your employer's rules on client data before you share matter details.

faq.question: Are research alerts free?
faq.answer: The Florida Coastal library guide says research alerts are free. Confirm this against your own plan, because product terms change over time.

costs.title: Money the firm absorbs
costs.text: When an out-of-plan charge is not passed to a client, the firm pays it. That cost sits in overhead, where nobody on the matter sees it. The total is hard to measure from outside, so start by reading the research line on your own statements each month.

costs.title: Margin on fixed-fee matters
costs.text: On a fixed-fee matter, every dollar of research counts against your margin. A quick session with extra document clicks can cost more than the searches themselves. The bill does not show that difference, so you only notice it when the matter closes.

costs.title: Time spent cleaning up
costs.text: Someone has to reconcile research charges to matters. That means checking Client IDs, sorting statements, and answering questions from billing. A surprise line on a client invoice also starts a conversation nobody planned for, and that conversation takes time too.

causes.title: The plan covers less than you think
causes.text: Thomson Reuters defines out-of-plan charges as document charges outside your subscription plan. They apply when you retrieve or deliver documents your plan does not include. The help page names Westlaw Classic, Westlaw Edge, and Practical Law. Check which plan your firm bought before you assume a result is covered.

causes.title: One click can open a billable document
causes.text: A law library guide says clicking a document on Lexis or Westlaw can trigger a charge. Results pages invite clicks, and skimming by opening everything in new tabs multiplies the risk. Most of these charges come from habit, not from one big decision.

causes.title: Citator reports pull in documents
causes.text: The same guide says citator reports carry charges in both systems when you click documents from them. Some Westlaw plans also charge extra for KeyCite. A check that looks like one step can turn into several billable clicks before you notice.

causes.title: Nobody tracks the session
causes.text: Without a Client ID, a session has no owner. Tulane Law Library's FAQ says the Client ID tracks which client to bill for a research session. If you forget it, or use one ID for everything, the charge loses its link to the matter.

causes.title: The firm treats research as overhead
causes.text: A 2014 State Bar of Wisconsin article says many firms now view computerized legal research as a cost of doing business, not a client-recoverable cost. When nobody expects to bill it, nobody watches it. That is why the charge can feel invisible until the statement arrives.

causes.title: The rate sheet is hard to find
causes.text: Rates follow the subscriber pricing guide, and the Westlaw help page gives no dollar amounts. Many lawyers never see that guide. Without the rate, nobody can tell whether a session was expensive or ordinary.

fixes.title: Ask for the rate in writing
fixes.text: Email your firm's research or billing lead. Ask for the subscriber pricing guide that matches your plan, and the rate for one out-of-plan document. Keep the reply with your matter notes. A written rate turns a vague worry into a number you can use.

fixes.title: Browse the table of contents first
fixes.text: The Florida Coastal guide says browsing the table of contents avoids the per-search charge. Start from the table of contents when you know the section you need. Open a document only when the table points to it. You make fewer clicks, and your research gets more precise.

fixes.title: Print from the browser, then confirm
fixes.text: The same guide says printing from the browser avoids document delivery fees. Use ⌘P to print the page you already have. On the print sheet, choose PDF > Save as PDF if you want a copy. Confirm on your plan first, because printing may be treated differently.

fixes.title: Set the Client ID before every session
fixes.text: Find the Client ID field in your research platform before you run a search. Tulane's FAQ says it tracks which client to bill. Use one ID per matter. A wrong ID sends the charge to the wrong client, which is harder to fix than a blank one.

fixes.title: Use research alerts for repeat topics
fixes.text: The guide says research alerts are free. If you check the same topic every week, set an alert instead of rerunning the search. Alerts bring new results to you without a fresh session, so you avoid repeat clicks.

fixes.title: Confirm Lexis terms in writing
fixes.text: The guide says Lexis Advance had no document delivery fee. Lexis products and terms change, so an older library guide is not a contract. Ask your Lexis account contact, in writing, whether your current plan has a document delivery fee.

fixes.title: Write a firm rule for research billing
fixes.text: Decide with your firm whether research goes on client bills. The Wisconsin article cites ABA Formal Opinion 93-379 as allowing recovery of reasonably incurred expenses, including computer research. Put the rule in engagement letters, and follow your state's rules.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Get the rate in writing
plan.text: Email your research or billing lead. Ask for the subscriber pricing guide that matches your plan, and the rate for one out-of-plan document. Ask whether Lexis has a document delivery fee on your contract. Save the replies in one folder.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check the Client ID first
plan.text: Find the Client ID field and confirm it before you run a search. Write the ID in your research log. If you forget, note the session so billing can fix it before the statement closes.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Browse first, then open
plan.text: On one real matter, start from the table of contents. Count how many documents you open, and note why you opened each one. Compare that with your usual pattern of clicks.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set alerts for repeat topics
plan.text: If you check the same topic each week, set a research alert instead. The Florida Coastal guide says alerts are free. Remove any recurring search you no longer need.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Match the log to the statement
plan.text: Compare your log with the research lines on the month's statement. Flag any charge you cannot explain. Send billing the matter number and date, and ask for a fix before invoices go out.
